chapter_title: Finite State Machines in Embedded Systems

screens.title: Finite State Machines in Embedded Systems
screens.subtitle: Modeling reactive behavior with states, inputs, transitions, and outputs

narration.text: In this chapter we learn a core design pattern used across embedded projects: the finite state machine. A finite state machine is a compact way to describe how a device reacts over time by being in one of a limited number of states, accepting inputs, making transitions, and producing outputs. This matters because embedded systems often need predictable, testable behavior for simple controllers like traffic lights, vending machines, or door locks. You will see how to draw state transition diagrams, map them to readable C code using a state variable and a switch statement, and choose between Moore and Mealy styles when you decide where outputs belong. I will guide you through concrete examples — the traffic light and a vending machine — and practical tasks you can implement on a LaunchPad with LEDs and switches. As you work, pay attention to common mistakes, like tying outputs directly to inputs instead of states, and the small structural choices that make FSM code easier to test and extend. By the end you will know how to represent behavior visually and translate that representation into reliable, maintainable embedded code.

keyIdea.title: Why FSMs matter
keyIdea.text: Finite state machines give embedded controllers a structured, predictable way to manage modes and reactions, making systems easier to reason about, test, and extend.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives set a clear path for practical competence. First, you will be able to define a finite state machine and name its four components: states, inputs, transitions, and outputs. That definition gives you the language to describe behavior precisely. Second, you will draw state transition diagrams for simple systems. Drawing diagrams is not art — it is a specification that you can test and implement. Third, you will implement an FSM in C using a state variable and a switch statement. That skill turns a diagram into running embedded code on a LaunchPad or equivalent board. Fourth, you will explain the difference between Moore and Mealy machines and decide when each style is preferable. Each objective includes a small verification task you can complete: define the FSM for a door lock on paper, then write the switch-based code and explain whether outputs belong to states or to inputs. These objectives focus on actionable skills: reading diagrams, writing predictable C code, and reasoning about outputs for reliable embedded behavior.

screens.title: What is a Finite State Machine?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and the four building blocks

narration.text: A finite state machine, or FSM, is a mathematical model describing systems that can be in exactly one of a finite set of states at any moment. The FSM reacts to inputs by applying transition rules that may change the current state and may trigger outputs. The four canonical components are states, inputs, transitions, and outputs. States are named conditions that represent meaningful system modes, like Green, Yellow, and Red in a traffic light. Inputs are events or conditions such as a timer expiring or a button press. Transitions are the rules that say when and how to move from one state to another given an input. Outputs are actions produced either when the system is in a state or when transitions occur. A useful way to reason about outputs is to ask: does the output depend only on the current state, or does it also depend on the input that caused the transition? That question leads directly to Moore and Mealy distinctions. A common misconception is to think that state and output are identical; they are related but distinct. States describe mode, and outputs are the signals you assert to represent or act on that mode. Keep this separation clear, and your designs will be easier to test, because you can assert state coverage and output expectations independently.

keyIdea.title: FSM as a precise specification
keyIdea.text: An FSM separates stateful modes from inputs and outputs so behavior is unambiguous and testable.

content.html:
Core Concept What is an FSM?
Definition and the four components
A precise vocabulary that makes embedded behavior predictable.
Quick definition

An FSM is a system that occupies one of a finite number of named states, reacts to inputs, and transitions between states while producing outputs.

States
Named conditions that represent modes of operation.
Inputs
Events or signals that can trigger transitions.
Transitions
Rules that move the machine from one state to another.
Outputs
Signals produced either by states or transitions, depending on style.
Explanation and example
  • Think of a traffic light: Green, Yellow, Red are states; the timer is an input that causes transitions.
  • Transitions are labeled by the triggering input, for example timer expires leads from Green to Yellow.
  • Outputs may be LED signals that show the current state or may be pulses emitted on transitions.
Example
Traffic light uses three states and a periodic timer input to cycle through them predictably.
Common mistake
Confusing a state name with an output. State is a mode; outputs are signals used to represent or act on that mode.
Key Takeaway

An FSM separates what mode the system is in from what events cause moves and what signals get produced, making behavior explicit.

screens.title: Drawing State Transition Diagrams
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step process for clear, testable diagrams

narration.text: Drawing a state transition diagram is the first engineering step in designing an FSM. Start by listing all meaningful states — do not invent transient labels; states should represent observable modes. Next, list inputs the system will respond to, such as timers, button presses, or sensor thresholds. Third, for each state and each input, decide whether the input causes a transition and where it goes; write these as arrows labeled by the input condition. Fourth, mark initial state and any terminal or error states. A concrete example is a traffic light: list Green, Yellow, Red; identify timer as the single input; then draw arrows from Green to Yellow, Yellow to Red, and Red back to Green, each labeled timer expires. A common misconception is to include too many states that differ only by output timing; prefer fewer states and model timing as inputs or counters. Finally, use your diagram to produce test cases: for each arrow, write a test that asserts that when the FSM is in the source state and the input occurs, the system reaches the correct target state. That test-driven habit prevents mismatches between design and implementation.

keyIdea.title: Diagram-driven design
keyIdea.text: Use diagrams as executable specifications: list states, list inputs, draw labeled arrows, mark initial state, and derive tests for each transition.

content.html:
Process Flow Draw diagrams
Steps to a clear state transition diagram
Turn behavior into a testable visual specification.
Step-by-step
  1. List meaningful states that represent distinct modes.
  2. List inputs and events that cause change.
  3. Draw arrows for transitions, label each with the triggering input.
  4. Mark the initial state and design tests for each transition.
Test derivation
For every labeled arrow, write a test: given source state and input, expect target state and expected outputs.
Concrete example — Traffic light
States: Green, Yellow, Red. Input: timer expires. Transitions: Green leads to Yellow, Yellow leads to Red, Red leads to Green.
Example Test
When in Green and timer expires, expect Yellow and the yellow output asserted.
Common Mistake
Creating states for timing phases rather than modeling time as an input leads to brittle designs.
Key Takeaway

A clear diagram becomes a precise test plan: each arrow corresponds to a verifiable behavior.

screens.title: Traffic Light FSM — Specification and Tests
screens.subtitle: Specify the traffic light and derive tests that validate each transition

narration.text: The traffic light is the canonical FSM example for embedded students because it is concrete and immediately observable. Start by specifying the states Green, Yellow, Red and the single input, a periodic timer. Write the transitions: when the timer expires in Green, go to Yellow; when the timer expires in Yellow, go to Red; when the timer expires in Red, go to Green. From this diagram you can derive simple tests: for each source state, simulate the timer input and assert the new state and output LEDs. Implementing these tests helps reveal errors such as forgetting to set the output when entering a state or mislabeling a transition. Another practical consideration is the initial state: choose Green and test that the system asserts the green output immediately after reset. A common misconception is to conflate the timer edge with output timing; remember that the timer is an input event, and the output should reflect the resulting state. This clarity makes both the running device and your unit tests readable and reliable. Traffic Light FSM — Specification and Tests means translate the simple traffic light diagram into tests that assert correct state transitions and outputs after simulated inputs.. In practical terms, specify the traffic light and derive tests that validate each transition. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Traffic light as a test bed
keyIdea.text: Translate the simple traffic light diagram into tests that assert correct state transitions and outputs after simulated inputs.

content.html:
Example Traffic Light FSM
Specification and simple tests
Concrete states, inputs, transitions, and observable outputs.
Specification
  • States: Green, Yellow, Red.
  • Input: timer expires.
  • Transitions: Green → Yellow → Red → Green on timer events.
  • Initial state: Green after reset.
Derived Test
Simulate being in Red, apply timer input, expect Green and green output asserted.
Practical notes
  • Ensure the initial state sets outputs so observers can read the state from LEDs.
  • Test each arrow to avoid off-by-one timing errors between transitions.
  • Keep timing inputs separate from state representation to avoid brittle designs.
Example
Run on a LaunchPad: three LEDs map to states; timer input can be simulated by a periodic interrupt or a switch during testing.
Pitfall
Assuming outputs change before state updates can cause wrong observations; define when outputs get asserted relative to state change.
Key Takeaway

Use the traffic light to practice deriving tests from diagrams and ensure initial state and output assertions are explicit.

screens.title: Implementing FSMs in C
screens.subtitle: Enum state, state variable, and switch-based handler pattern

narration.text: A common and clear implementation pattern in embedded C is an enum that lists states, a module-level state variable, and a handler function that uses a switch statement on the current state. The code structure follows the FSM principles: read inputs, check the current state, apply transition rules, set the new state, and update outputs. For example, a traffic light enum lists GREEN, YELLOW, RED and the handler checks if the timer expired; if so it assigns the next state and asserts the corresponding LED. This structure is regular and easy to test because each case corresponds to one state. One helpful practice is to include a default case that resets to a safe initial state to recover from unexpected values. Another pattern is to keep output updates grouped when entering states rather than scattered across transitions; that makes the code closer to a Moore machine and easier to observe. A common misconception is that switch statements make code messy; when used as a direct mapping from a diagram, they become clear documentation of behavior. Finally, this pattern scales: to add a state or a transition, add one enum entry and one switch case or a new branch in an existing case, then update tests to cover the new arrows.

keyIdea.title: Regular structure
keyIdea.text: Use an enum, a state variable, and a switch handler so each state maps to a readable case and tests map to cases.

content.html:
Implementation C switch-based FSM
Enum, state variable, and a switch handler
A pattern that maps diagram states directly to code cases.
Code pattern (illustrative)
typedef enum { GREEN, YELLOW, RED } TrafficLightState;
TrafficLightState state = GREEN;

void trafficLightFSM(uint8_t timerExpired) {
    switch (state) {
        case GREEN:
            if (timerExpired) { state = YELLOW; setYellowLED(); }
            break;
        case YELLOW:
            if (timerExpired) { state = RED; setRedLED(); }
            break;
        case RED:
            if (timerExpired) { state = GREEN; setGreenLED(); }
            break;
        default:
            state = GREEN;
            break;
    }
}
Explanation and practices
  • Each switch case corresponds to a single state and contains transition logic for inputs.
  • Group output updates when entering a state to resemble a Moore machine and improve observability.
  • Include a default case that returns to a safe initial state to handle corruption or unexpected values.
Pro Tip
Keep state modification and output updates close together so tests can assert both the new state and output signals.
Key Takeaway

Translate diagram arrows to switch cases and keep code structure regular for easier extension and testing.

screens.title: Moore vs Mealy Machines
screens.subtitle: How outputs are produced and why it matters

narration.text: Two common FSM styles are Moore machines and Mealy machines. In a Moore machine, outputs depend only on the current state; when you are in a state, you know exactly which outputs will be asserted. That makes timing predictable and observations easy: read the outputs to infer the state. In a Mealy machine, outputs depend on both the current state and the current input, so the same state can produce different outputs depending on the input that just arrived. Mealy machines can be more compact because you can emit outputs as part of transitions, but they are also more sensitive to input timing and can be harder to test because outputs are transient and depend on the occurrence of inputs. In embedded practice, Moore machines are often preferred because of clarity and testability: the output is a steady reflection of state. A typical misconception is that Mealy is always faster; while Mealy can react immediately to inputs, the trade-off in testability and timing discipline may outweigh that benefit for many controllers. Moore vs Mealy Machines means moore ties outputs to state for predictability; mealy ties outputs to state and input for compact transitions. choose based on timing and testability needs.. In practical terms, how outputs are produced and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design choice
keyIdea.text: Moore ties outputs to state for predictability; Mealy ties outputs to state and input for compact transitions. Choose based on timing and testability needs.

content.html:
Comparison Moore vs Mealy
Where outputs come from matters
Trade timing and compactness against clarity and testability.
Moore Machine
Outputs depend only on the current state. Observers can read outputs to infer state. Easier to test and reason about.
When to use
When predictable outputs and testability are priorities.
Misconception
Thinking Moore is always slower; it's often clearer which improves reliability.
Mealy Machine
Outputs depend on state and current inputs. Can respond immediately to events and reduce state count, but outputs may be transient and timing-sensitive.
When to use
When you need immediate reactions tied to specific inputs and accept more complex testing.
Pro Tip
Document whether outputs are state-driven or input-driven so testers know what to assert.
Key Takeaway

Choose Moore for clarity and testability; choose Mealy for compact, immediate reactions and when transient outputs are acceptable.

screens.title: Vending Machine: Multiple Inputs and States
screens.subtitle: Mapping coins, selections, and cancel signals into a structured FSM

narration.text: When an FSM has multiple inputs, design clarity becomes even more important. Consider a vending machine: candidate states include Idle, CoinInserted, SelectionMade, Dispensing, and ChangeReturned. Inputs include coin inserted, button pressed, and cancel pressed. For each state, enumerate which inputs are relevant and where they lead. For example, from Idle a coin inserted leads to CoinInserted; from CoinInserted a selection leads to Dispensing if sufficient credit exists; a cancel pressed returns to ChangeReturned. Implementing this in C typically means reading multiple input signals and evaluating them in the active state's case. One practical tip is to consolidate input processing into a small helper that returns a single input code or flag set so the switch logic stays readable. A common mistake is scattering input handling across the codebase rather than keeping transition logic centralized. Centralizing makes test cases easier to write: for each source state and input combination, you can assert the expected next state and expected outputs, such as a motor on or coin return pulse. Keeping the FSM structure clear will pay off as complexity grows. Vending Machine: Multiple Inputs and States means for multiple inputs, keep transition rules centralized per state so each case cleanly expresses what inputs matter and where they lead.. In practical terms, mapping coins, selections, and cancel signals into a structured fsm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Centralize transitions
keyIdea.text: For multiple inputs, keep transition rules centralized per state so each case cleanly expresses what inputs matter and where they lead.

content.html:
Architecture Vending Machine FSM
States and multiple inputs
Design transitions so each input is handled in the relevant state only.
Suggested states
  • Idle — waiting for a coin.
  • CoinInserted — credit recorded, waiting for selection.
  • SelectionMade — checking inventory and price.
  • Dispensing — motor or actuator running.
  • ChangeReturned — returning unused credit.
Input list
coin inserted, button pressed, cancel pressed, and internal timers or sensors.
Implementation notes
  • Map input signals to an input code before the switch to keep cases compact.
  • Centralize transition rules inside each case so behavior is easy to read and test.
  • Handle unexpected inputs by remaining in the current state or moving to a safe fallback.
Example transition
From CoinInserted, if button pressed and credit sufficient, go to Dispensing and start motor output.
Common Mistake
Scattering input handling across functions makes it hard to ensure full transition coverage in tests.
Key Takeaway

Centralize input decoding and keep transition logic per state so tests can enumerate source state plus input to assert outcomes.

screens.title: Door Lock FSM — Design and Implementation Task
screens.subtitle: Locked, Unlocked, Alarm with code entry, wrong code, and timeout

narration.text: This hands-on task ties the chapter together. Design a door lock FSM with three states: Locked, Unlocked, and Alarm. Inputs are correct code entered, wrong code entered, and timeout. On correct code entered while Locked, transition to Unlocked and assert the unlocked output. On wrong code entered in Locked, either stay in Locked or, after repeated wrong attempts, transition to Alarm. On timeout while Unlocked, transition to Locked to re-secure the system. Start by drawing the diagram and labeling the arrows with the specific inputs. Then implement the FSM in C using an enum, a state variable, and a switch handler. Use LaunchPad switches to simulate code entry and LEDs to show Locked, Unlocked, and Alarm states. A practical implementation note: debounce and validate inputs before feeding them to the FSM so transient switch noise does not trigger unintended transitions. Finally, write tests for each arrow: given initial state and input, assert the new state and expected outputs. This exercise emphasizes the full design loop from diagram to hardware verification. Door Lock FSM — Design and Implementation Task means design the diagram, implement the switch-based handler, and verify each transition on hardware or in unit tests.. In practical terms, locked, unlocked, alarm with code entry, wrong code, and timeout. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Full design loop
keyIdea.text: Design the diagram, implement the switch-based handler, and verify each transition on hardware or in unit tests.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Door Lock FSM
Design, implement, and test on hardware
A compact exercise to practice full FSM workflow.
Design steps
  1. List states: Locked, Unlocked, Alarm.
  2. List inputs: correct code, wrong code, timeout.
  3. Draw arrows and mark initial state Locked.
  4. Derive tests for each arrow and initial behavior after reset.
Implementation note
Debounce and validate switches before passing events to the FSM to avoid spurious transitions.
Testing and verification
  • Test initial reset asserts Locked output and no transitions without inputs.
  • Simulate correct code input and assert Unlocked is reached and LED shows unlocked.
  • Simulate repeated wrong entries and verify Alarm triggers if designed to do so.
Concrete mapping
Use an enum for states, a single state variable, and a switch in the main loop or interrupt handler for transitions.
Pitfall
Not testing the initial state after reset can hide mis-initialization bugs where outputs do not match the expected mode.
Key Takeaway

This activity reinforces diagram-first design, then code mapping, then test-based verification on real hardware.

screens.title: Testing FSMs: Coverage and Edge Cases
screens.subtitle: Derive tests from diagrams and watch for hidden transitions

narration.text: Testing an FSM starts with the diagram. Each labeled arrow becomes a test scenario: given the system is in the source state and the specified input occurs, assert the system reaches the target state and that outputs match expectations. Aim for transition coverage so every arrow is exercised. Also test initial state after reset and error handling paths. Edge cases include simultaneous inputs and inputs during transitions; decide how your design should prioritize or queue inputs and test that behavior explicitly. A helpful debugging practice is to add logging or LED blink patterns that indicate current state so you can observe misbehavior easily on hardware. Another common bug is forgetting to handle unexpected input combinations or neglecting the default case in a switch, which can leave the state variable with an invalid value; include a default that resets to a safe initial state. Finally, write tests that simulate repeated inputs and noisy signals to ensure debouncing and input validation prevent false transitions. Designing tests from the diagram turns a visual spec into rigorous validation steps. Testing FSMs: Coverage and Edge Cases means convert every arrow into a test, include initial and error cases, and simulate noisy or simultaneous inputs to validate robustness.. In practical terms, derive tests from diagrams and watch for hidden transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Diagram-to-test mapping
keyIdea.text: Convert every arrow into a test, include initial and error cases, and simulate noisy or simultaneous inputs to validate robustness.

content.html:
Testing & Debugging FSM Test Strategy
From diagram to test cases
Ensure transition coverage and robustness against noise.
Test checklist
  • For each transition: source state + input → expected target state and outputs.
  • Initial state after reset asserted and outputs visible.
  • Invalid or unexpected inputs lead to safe fallback or no transition.
  • Simultaneous or noisy inputs are debounced and tested.
Debugging tips
Use simple LED patterns or serial logs to indicate current state for easier diagnosis on hardware.
Include a default handler to recover from invalid state values.
Write tests that emulate repeated inputs and transitions to reveal timing bugs.
Common Pitfall

Not testing initial state or default handling can hide silent failures that only appear in the field.

screens.title: Scaling and Extending State Machines
screens.subtitle: Adding states and managing complexity the right way

narration.text: As systems grow, so do FSMs. Adding states and transitions should be deliberate: update the state enum, add or modify the corresponding switch cases, and extend your tests so new transitions are covered. A lightweight approach is to group related behavior into sub-states or to implement a table-driven FSM when the number of states and inputs becomes large. The chapter content emphasizes that to add a new state you add a new case to the switch statement, but this simple step can lead to messy code if you do not keep transitions organized. Use clear naming for states and keep transition logic compact by decoding inputs before the switch. Another strategy for complexity management is to factor common actions into helper functions, such as entry and exit actions for states, so the switch remains a concise map from state to behavior. A common misconception is that more states automatically mean better granularity; instead, choose states that capture meaningful modes, and model timing or counters as inputs to avoid exploding the state space. Always follow the diagram-to-test pipeline when extending so nothing slips through untested.

keyIdea.title: Controlled growth
keyIdea.text: Add states deliberately, keep switch cases tidy, and extend tests to preserve clarity as complexity grows.

content.html:
Hierarchy Scaling FSMs
Strategies for growing state machines
Keep the structure readable and tests comprehensive.
Practical strategies
  • Keep state enums small and meaningful; model timing or counts as inputs.
  • Decode inputs before the switch to keep cases concise.
  • Factor entry and exit actions into helpers to avoid duplication.
When to refactor
If switch cases grow large, consider a table-driven approach or nested sub-states to manage complexity.
Always update and run tests when adding transitions so new behavior is validated.
Key Takeaway

Scale FSMs by keeping state names meaningful, centralizing input decoding, and factoring repeated actions into helpers for maintainability.

screens.title: Why Use FSMs and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Benefits for embedded control and what to avoid

narration.text: Finite state machines bring structure and predictability to embedded controllers. The advantages are clear: FSMs make behavior explicit, they are easy to document with diagrams, and they map directly to readable C code using enums and switch statements. This regular structure simplifies testing because every state and transition can be enumerated and covered with unit tests. However, common mistakes reduce those benefits. One mistake is overusing states to model minor timing differences; instead model time as an input or counter. Another is scattering output updates across multiple functions, which makes tests harder to write because you cannot tell where outputs are asserted. Forgetting a default case in the switch can leave the state variable in an invalid value after corruption or a bug, so always include a safe fallback. Lastly, confusing Moore and Mealy styles leads to wrong timing assumptions; pick a style and document it so tests assert the correct expectations. Using FSMs thoughtfully keeps embedded logic maintainable and verifiable. Why Use FSMs and Common Mistakes means fsms improve clarity and testability when states are meaningful and transition logic is centralized; avoid modeling timing as extra states.. In practical terms, benefits for embedded control and what to avoid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use FSMs thoughtfully
keyIdea.text: FSMs improve clarity and testability when states are meaningful and transition logic is centralized; avoid modeling timing as extra states.

content.html:
Summary Advantages & Pitfalls
Why choose FSMs and common errors to avoid
Structure yields maintainability when used correctly.
Advantages
  • Explicit behavioral specification.
  • Direct mapping to readable C code.
  • Easy to enumerate tests for each transition.
Common Pitfalls
  • Using states to capture timing leads to state explosion.
  • Scattered output updates make testing difficult.
  • Missing default case allows invalid states to persist.
Key Takeaway

FSMs are powerful for embedded control when states are meaningful, transitions are centralized, and tests exercise each arrow.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Here are the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, every FSM has four components: states, inputs, transitions, and outputs. Naming each clearly allows you to describe behavior unambiguously. Second, draw state transition diagrams that label arrows with triggering inputs; use the diagram as a test plan so each arrow becomes a test case. Third, implement FSMs in C by using an enum for states, a state variable, and a switch statement that acts as the state handler. This yields readable, testable code. Fourth, distinguish Moore from Mealy: Moore outputs depend only on state, Mealy outputs depend on state and input. Choose Moore when observability and testability matter. Finally, centralize transition logic, include a default fallback, and avoid modeling timing as additional states. These practices keep embedded controllers predictable and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: States, inputs, transitions, outputs; diagram first, implement with enum and switch, pick Moore or Mealy consciously.

content.html:
What to Remember
Three compact concept cards
FSM Components
States, inputs, transitions, outputs are the vocabulary for describing behavior.
Diagram-First
Diagrams are executable specifications; each arrow should map to a test case.
Implement in C
Use an enum for states and a switch handler to map states to transition logic and outputs.
Summary
Keep FSMs simple and testable: diagram, implement, and verify each transition; choose Moore for clarity and Mealy for immediate, input-driven outputs.

Second, include a default case in switch handlers to recover to a safe state if the state variable becomes invalid. Third, centralize input decoding so switch cases remain concise and transition rules are easy to read. Fourth, document whether outputs are produced by state alone or by state plus input so tests assert the correct timing. Fifth, derive tests directly from the diagram: one test per arrow plus initial and error cases. These habits reduce ambiguity and make embedded controllers reliable in hardware and simulation. What to Remember
Practical checklist
Quick rules to follow as you implement FSMs.
Initialize State
Set the initial state and outputs after reset so the system is observable.
Default Fallback
Include a default case to recover from invalid or corrupted state values.
Centralize Decoding
Decode inputs before the switch so cases remain focused on transitions and outputs.
Final Note
Derive tests from your diagram and update them whenever you add states or transitions to keep behavior verified.
